summary: This incident report explains how redundant systems (hardware, network and geographic duplication) keep telecom services running during failures. It cites real-world examples from late 2023, including a severed fiber line in Los Angeles, an East Coast power outage and an attempted cyber-attack on QuickNet. It also covers redundancy architecture, the role of human operators, future needs with IoT and 5G, and the cost and complexity of implementing redundancy.
one_line: Report on how redundant telecom systems prevented major outages in 2023 incidents, plus their architecture, challenges and future importance.
key_facts: Redundancy in telecommunications means duplicating critical components or systems so that if one path or element fails, another takes over without the end-user perceiving an interruption.
The report names three levels of redundancy: hardware redundancy, network redundancy (different data paths), and geographic redundancy (services mirrored in separate physical locations).

On September 15, 2023, a construction mishap in downtown Los Angeles severed a major fiber optic line, and GlobalCom Inc.'s redundant systems redirected data flow through alternative channels, keeping service uninterrupted.

On October 8, 2023, a large-scale power outage hit the East Coast from Washington D.C. to New York City; redundant power sources such as battery backups and diesel generators kept key network hubs operational until the grid was restored, according to Johnathan Bridges.
Johnathan Bridges is a network engineer with over a decade of experience who said that without redundant power sources thousands of businesses would have experienced communication failures.
On November 21, 2023, ISP QuickNet faced an attempted cyber-attack that was mitigated through redundant security measures and quick response protocols, with no service disruption.

Angela Martinez, SwiftLink Telecommunications' Senior Infrastructure Architect, said redundancy runs from the physical layer up to the application layer, with each stage having its own redundancy protocol.

The report describes three architectural elements: component-level redundancy (switches, routers, servers), route diversity (different physical paths and mediums such as satellite links), and geographical redundancy (data centers and server farms in different regions).
Network operation centers (NOCs) are staffed 24/7 by technicians and engineers whose decision-making is essential to promptly applying redundant systems during crises.

Analyst Diana Thompson said operators that prioritize redundancy investments will set industry standards and earn customer loyalty, after observing network resilience during storms in early December 2023.
Implementing redundancy is costly and complex because of duplicated hardware, multiple data paths and diverse geographic locations, and the challenges are more pronounced for small-scale providers.
The report concludes that redundancy is 'not a luxury but a necessity,' and expects its importance to grow with the Internet of Things (IoT) and 5G networks.
